scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Gending Sriwijaya was created between 1943 and 1944 during the Japanese occupation era to meet a government request to the Information Bureau (Hatching) for a dance and song to welcome official visitors to the Palembang Residency in South Sumatra, Indonesia.
The dance choreography was developed by Tina Haji Gong and Sukadan A. Rozak, who drew upon existing traditional Palembang dance elements.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Gending Sriwijaya is a ceremonial welcoming dance designed to demonstrate hospitality, sincerity, and cultural refinement.
It is performed before heads of state, foreign ambassadors, ministers, kings, queens, and VIP guests during state dinners, luncheons, and official receptions.
The central ritual—the offering of betel nut (bersirih or menginang)—re-enacts court traditions once reserved for royal princesses.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is based on the simpler Tanggai dance and models a traditional court welcoming protocol.
A troupe of nine female dancers—representing Srivijaya princesses—performs alongside two male guards (pengawal) carrying yellow parasols and gilded spears.
At the center of the formation is a prime lady who wears the most elaborate costume and holds a tepak container filled with betel leaf, areca nut, and slaked lime (Sekapur Sirih).
Watch for Sekapur Sirih Offering.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The performance is set to the Gending Sriwijaya composition, traditionally played by a live ensemble of gamelan instruments and gongs accompanied by a vocal soloist singing lyrics authored by Nungcik AR.
Composer A. Dahlan Muhabat blended local melodies with Japanese musical structural influences to craft the song.
Listen for the Gamelan, Gongs, Violin.
A stately blend of classical gamelan percussion, gongs, and vocal song, historically composed using violin and fusing traditional Palembang court melodies with mid-20th-century structural influences.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear the traditional, highly ornate Aesan Gede songket costume, accented with Selendang Mantri, Paksangkong, Dodot, and gilded tanggai finger covers.
The visual style reflects a fusion of Malay, Javanese, and Chinese cultural influences.
Stage settings typically involve formal ceremonial venues, state banquets, high-level reception halls, or open-air festival stages such as the annual Festival Sriwijaya in Palembang.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures in the creation of Gending Sriwijaya include dance stylists Tina Haji Gong and Sukadan A. Rozak, composer A. Dahlan Muhabat, and lyricist Nungcik AR.

While Gending Sriwijaya itself represents a formalized Palembang state dance, it is directly based on the simpler Tanggai dance of South Sumatra and is related to other regional welcoming dances like the Kebagh dance and Melinting dance.

Rooted in historic Srivijayan court practices and Palembang folk traditions, Gending Sriwijaya evolved out of the Tanggai dance during the mid-20th century, retaining direct links to traditional Malay betel-offering rituals (Sekapur Sirih).
